newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian president might break deadlock.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian president might break deadlock.

text.p: Bulgaria's beleaguered government and an angry mass protest movement demanding elections awaited the swearing-in on Sunday of a new president likely to break their bitter political deadlock.

Incoming President Petar Stoyanov has said he may grant the ruling Socialists the mandate to form a new cabinet denied them by predecessor Zhelyu Zhelev. The opposition vehemently opposes a new mandate and wants elections as soon as possible.

Stoyanov's inauguration is itself a potential flashpoint. Government officials appealed to Sofia's opposition Mayor Stefan Sofianski to guarantee public order around the parliament building while it takes place.

Anti-government protesters, angered by 300 percent inflation that has reduced millions of Bulgarians to paupers, besieged and ransacked the building last weekend in clashes with riot police in which 196 people were injured.
Leaders of trades unions and the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) called on supporters to rally near the parliament at four p.m. (1400 gmt) after the swearing-in ceremony.
Stoyanov is not a Socialist but has said he will reluctantly ask the Socialists to form a government if they cannot reach agreement with the opposition on an interim cabinet.
"Granting a mandate to the Socialists is not going to solve the crisis, nor make people return to their homes," he said in an interview with Spain's El Pais daily.
Echoing proposals by UDF leader Ivan Kostov for polls by the end of March, he said spring elections "may be one of the most suitable options."
"What is needed is agreement between the political forces on at least one fundamental point: immediate economic reform," he said.
"The main problem is that no government will be able to control the situation in Bulgaria if it doesn't receive the support of the current or future opposition."
Zhelev told Bulgarian television: "There is no sense in handing a formal mandate which will explode social peace."
The government of former communists, mired in a deep economic crisis blamed on its ineptitude and corruption, scored a mere eight percent support in one opinion poll last week.
The strain of 13 days of mass demonstrations and strikes showed when four dissident Socialist deputies joined a new rival leftist coalition.

New Left in Bulgaria, formed by the Socialists' reformist wing and a small liberal Marxist party, said it wanted economic reform of the kind introduced in most of ex-communist eastern Europe but which has barely begun in Bulgaria.
The Socialist divisions fuelled speculation that the party could lose its parliamentary majority, won in 1994 elections, even if granted a new mandate by Stoyanov.

Students danced in Sofia's streets, ethnic Turks and gypsies rallied and taxis jammed the Danube town of Rousse on Saturday to protest against economic misery and demand elections not constitutionally required for almost two years.
"They beat us with truncheons, we will beat them with elections," one student placard read.
Diplomats say a delay in holding elections could aid the Socialists as the polls would be held after a new accord with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) which might be bearing fruit.
The IMF has said it will complete talks on introducing a tight monetary regime, its condition for handing over financial aid, with a new government as soon as it is formed.
The collapsing lev currency fell to new lows below 700 to the dollar on Friday, down from 70 a year ago.
